title: Cults: Who is this "The Leader?"
summary: Josh and Chuck explore how cults work, focusing on destructive (totalist) cults versus religions, the charismatic leader, recruitment through stress and grief groups, isolation and thought reform (brainwashing), dependency and control, leaving a cult and deprogramming, and a tour of notable cases including Heaven's Gate, Jonestown, the Branch Davidians, the Manson family, the Order of the Solar Temple, the Raelians, and historical female cult leaders. The episode closes with a South by Southwest live show announcement and listener mail about an art-sharing project.

segments.title: Opening and Heaven's Gate overview
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode and recounts the 1997 Heaven's Gate mass suicides in Rancho Santa Fe, tied to the Hale-Bopp comet, noting the members' calm exit videos.

segments.title: Destructive cults vs. religion
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish destructive or totalist cults from mainstream religions, noting hierarchy, absolute commitment and control, and debate whether cult leaders truly believe their own message.

segments.title: Authoritarian leadership and the charismatic leader
segments.summary: Cults are typically run by one male leader operating outside the mainstream, with isolation, us-versus-them divides, and charismatic leaders claiming divine status. Members devote themselves to the leader rather than his ideas.

segments.title: Origins of cult leaders and personal histories
segments.summary: Many cult leaders start in mainstream religion, such as Jim Jones (Disciples of Christ) and David Koresh (Seventh-day Adventist). The hosts discuss their early sexual histories and how overzealousness leads to splintering off.

segments.title: Charles Manson and the Manson family
segments.summary: Charlie Manson is described as a non-religious manipulator who drew in hippies, ordered the Tate-LaBianca murders without committing them himself, and was convicted in California. Squeaky Fromme's attempt on Gerald Ford is also mentioned.

segments.title: Who joins cults: recruitment and vulnerability
segments.summary: Cult members are not generally mentally ill; they are usually recruited during stressful life events and may be gullible, unassertive, or seeking spiritual meaning. Recruiting often happens in grief support groups and through trusted members.

segments.title: Deception, isolation and thought reform
segments.summary: Recruiters hide the group's true nature, isolate recruits in retreats and meetings, limit outside feedback, and use thought reform (brainwashing, coercive persuasion) to break down the sense of self. The hosts compare it to interrogation and boot camp, noting boot camp's differences.

segments.title: Dependency, control, guilt and dread
segments.summary: Cults create dependency through love-bombing and guilt, strictly scheduled days, removal of decision-making, and stripping of talents. Members develop a lingering sense of dread and internal conflict between old and new selves. Former members often report anxiety and fear.

segments.title: Finances, leaving, deprogramming and exit counseling
segments.summary: Cults rely on member finances; leaving can be easy or blocked by isolation and shame. The hosts discuss the Branch Davidians' failed predicted dates, the Jonestown shooting of Congressman Leo Ryan, the Kool-Aid myth, and deprogramming and exit counseling, including the lasting aftereffects of leaving.

segments.title: Other notable cults and historical female leaders
segments.summary: Brief discussion of Ruby Ridge and Waco, the Order of the Solar Temple deaths in Switzerland and Canada, the Raelians, and female cult leaders including Joanna Southcott, Ann Lee and the Shakers, and Margaret Peter.

segments.title: Live show announcement and sign-off mail
segments.summary: Announcement of a live South by Southwest show and a listener mail item about an art sketchbook giveaway project, followed by a closing note.
